rc-literary.title: Literary
rc-literary.html:
Poems & Essays  ·  + tone & devices

A literary passage uses figurative language, tone and theme: essays, speeches, poems, reflections. Questions ask about tone, devices, theme and meaning of lines. Read for what the writer feels, not only what is said.

PAGE 1
Read for Meaning and ToneLiteral, figurative and the writer's attitude

Start here: What is the writer doing? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Literal or figurative? Then name the tone.

1.1 Tone words to know

POSITIVEadmiring, hopeful, joyful, appreciative, optimistic
NEGATIVEcritical, cynical, bitter, regretful, mournful
NEUTRALobjective, reflective, descriptive, thoughtful

1.2 Devices that carry meaning

SIMILE / METAPHORcompares to show an idea Time is a river.
PERSONIFICATIONgives life to things The wind sang.
IRONYopposite of the expected a fire station burning down.
M E M O R Y H A C K | W O R D C H O I C E = T O N E

Adjectives and verbs reveal tone. "clung to her old books" = nostalgic; "dismissed the idea" = dismissive.

PAGE 2
Question Types and Attack PlanTone, device, theme and meaning

2.1 Which question type? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Tone, meaning, theme, device.

2.2 Question types

TONEwriter's attitude admiring, critical, nostalgic
MEANING OF A LINEwhat is suggested find the idea behind the image
DEVICEwhy is it used? to make the idea vivid
THEMEthe central message what the whole says
INFERENCEwhat is implied stay close to the text
VOCABULARYword in context reread and substitute

2.3 Worked mini-example

Passage: "Grandmother's kitchen smelled of cardamom and old stories. I would give anything to sit there once more."

Q: WHAT IS THE TONE?

Tone. "give anything to sit there once more" = nostalgic.

Q: WHAT DOES "OLD STORIES" ADD?

Device. It gives the smell a feeling of memory and warmth.

E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Literal reading of a metaphor: "Time is a thief" does not mean time steals objects.

Wrong tone: "sad" is not the same as "bitter" or "nostalgic".

Over-reading: stay within the text.

M E M O R Y H A C K | I M A G E → I D E A

Turn every image into an idea. Sun dipping into the sea = the day ending. Locked door = no way forward.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Choose the tone or theme (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Feeling of the words, not literal reading.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY"Time is a thief" = time steals things "Time is a thief" = time takes away our days metaphor Tone = angry (for nostalgia) Tone = nostalgic longing for the past Theme = a detail Theme = central message whole text Device = random Device = makes the idea vivid effect Meaning = literal Meaning = figurative idea image to idea Tone = happy for a mournful passage Tone = mournful sad words Title = one image Title = whole idea covers the text Inference = wild guess Inference = close to text evidence

3.3 Mixed practice: strategy questions

1. "Time is a thief." Literal or figurative?

2. Longing for the past: which tone?

3. What do adjectives and verbs reveal?

4. What does a metaphor turn into?

5. "Sun dipping into the sea" suggests what?

6. Should you read a metaphor literally?

7. A theme covers one image or the whole text?

8. Which tone is "mournful"?

9. What does personification do?

10. How do you choose between close tone words?

Answers: 1 figurative, 2 nostalgic, 3 tone, 4 an idea, 5 the day ending, 6 no, 7 the whole text, 8 sad and sorrowful, 9 gives life to things, 10 check the strength of the words.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Literal or figurative?

Tone: adjectives and verbs.

Image → idea.

Theme: whole text, not a detail.

Do not read metaphors literally.

Choose the tone that matches the feeling and the strength.

Stay close to the text.

rc-factual.title: Factual
rc-factual.html:
Facts & Data  ·  + 6 question types

A factual passage informs: science, environment, economy, history. It has facts, figures and logical flow. The answers are in the passage, so match, do not guess.

PAGE 1
Read the Passage SmartlyStructure first, details later

Start here: How to read a factual passage (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Skim for structure, then read questions, then hunt the answers.

1.1 How a factual passage is built

TOPIC SENTENCEfirst line of a paragraph states the idea Water pollution is rising.
SUPPORTfacts, figures, examples In 2020, 40% of rivers...
CONCLUSIONlast lines summarise or advise Therefore, we must...

1.2 Signal words to watch

CONTRASThowever, but, although, yet the idea turns
CAUSE / RESULTbecause, so, therefore, as a result reasons and effects
ADDITION / EXAMPLEmoreover, for instance, such as more detail
M E M O R Y H A C K | T O P - D O W N R E A D I N G

First line, last line, every paragraph. Then read the questions. Then find the lines that answer them. You rarely need to read word by word.

PAGE 2
Question Types and Attack Plan
Six types and how to beat each

2.1 Which question type? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Name the question type, then use its method.

2.2 The six types

FACTanswer is stated Find the line, match the words.
INFERENCEanswer is implied Choose the safest conclusion.
MAIN IDEAwhat the whole passage says Use topic sentences.
VOCABULARYmeaning in context Substitute and test.
TONE / PURPOSEwriter's attitude objective, critical, hopeful.
TRUE / FALSEone option is a distortion Check each statement.

2.3 Worked mini-example

Passage: "Plastic takes up to 500 years to break down. Each year, about 8 million tonnes enter the oceans. However, recycling can cut this waste."

Q: HOW LONG DOES PLASTIC TAKE TO BREAK DOWN?

Fact. The passage says up to 500 years.

Q: WHAT IS THE WRITER'S TONE?

Tone. Facts first, then "however, recycling" = concerned but hopeful.

E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Extreme words (always, never, only, all) are usually wrong.

Right words, wrong idea: an option may reuse passage words but change the meaning.

Outside knowledge: answer only from the passage.

M E M O R Y H A C K | F I N D , M A T C H , C H E C K

Find the line, match the option to it, check that no word is stronger or different.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Eliminate options (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Eliminate extremes and outside ideas first.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYOption: "Plastic never breaks down" "Plastic breaks down in up to 500 years" extreme word
Option uses a new fact not in the passage
Choose the option stated or impliedoutside knowledge Main idea = one detail Main idea = the whole passage too narrow Inference = wild guess Inference = logical step stay close Tone = angry Tone = concerned check the words Vocabulary = dictionary meaning Vocabulary = meaning in the line context Title = a detail Title = covers the whole too small True / false: "all" statements Check qualifiers (some, many) distortion

3.3 Mixed practice: strategy questions

1. A question starts "According to the passage..." Which type is it?

2. An option says "always". What should you suspect?

3. You must pick the best title. What should it cover?

4. A word is asked "as used in the passage". What do you do?

5. An option uses facts not in the passage. Keep or eliminate?

6. Which part of a paragraph holds its main idea?

7. What does "however" signal?

8. "Which can be inferred?" asks for stated or implied?

9. Should you answer from your own knowledge?

10. Should you read the questions before or after skimming?

Answers: 1 fact, 2 it is too extreme, 3 the whole passage, 4 reread and substitute, 5 eliminate, 6 the first / last line, 7 a contrast, 8 implied, 9 no, 10 after skimming (then read questions, then hunt).

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Skim the structure (first and last lines).

Name the question type before answering.

Fact: find and match.

Inference: a short logical step.

Vocabulary: reread and substitute.

Eliminate extreme words and outside ideas.

Never answer from outside knowledge.

rc-narrative.title: Narrative
rc-narrative.html:
Story & Character  ·  + 5 clue types

A narrative passage tells a story: events, characters, setting and feeling. Questions ask who, why, how they felt and what happens next. Follow the events and the emotions.

PAGE 1
Read a Story PassageCharacter, setting, plot and mood

Start here: What is this passage about? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Who, what, how did they feel?

1.1 Parts of a narrative

CHARACTERwho the story is about traits shown by actions and words
SETTINGtime and place a rainy village night
PLOTorder of events problem → struggle → solution

1.2 Mood and tone words

POSITIVEjoyful, hopeful, proud, excited, grateful
NEGATIVEanxious, bitter, regretful, fearful, lonely
NEUTRALcalm, curious, thoughtful, matter-of-fact
MEMORY HACK | CHARACTER = ACTION + SPEECH

A character's trait is shown by what they do and say, not only what the writer calls them. "She ran back to help" = brave and kind.

PAGE 2
Question Types and Attack PlanInference, character, mood and sequence

2.1 Which question type? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Name the type: emotion, motive, prediction or theme.

2.2 Five types

CHARACTER TRAITwhat is the person like? read actions and speech
EMOTIONhow did he feel? adjectives, body signals
MOTIVEwhy did he act? look at the cause line
SEQUENCEwhat came first? time words
THEME / MORALthe lesson what changes by the end
VOCABULARYword in context reread and substitute

2.3 Worked mini-example

Passage: "Meena's hands shook as she opened the envelope. She read the first line, then burst into tears of joy. She had passed."

Q: HOW DID MEENA FEEL AT FIRST?

Emotion. "hands shook" = nervous.

Q: WHY DID SHE CRY?

Motive. "tears of joy... passed" = relief and happiness.

E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Reading too much in: choose what the text shows, not what you imagine.

Opposite feelings: "tears" can mean joy or sorrow; check the next words.

Sequence: use words like first, then, finally.

M E M O R Y H A C K | B O D Y S I G N A L S

Shaking hands = nervous. Smiling = pleased. Looking away = shy or guilty. Clenched fists = angry.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Decide the answer (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Keep what the text shows. Drop what you imagine.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYMeena felt angry (hands shook)
Meena felt nervousbody signal
She cried because she failed
She cried because she passedtears of joy Theme = a detail Theme = the big lesson whole story Motive = any reason Motive = reason in the text evidence Tone = sarcastic Tone = hopeful check words Sequence = guess Sequence = time words first, then Character = guess Character = actions and speech evidence Setting = mood Setting = time and place where and when

3.3 Mixed practice: strategy questions

1. "Her hands shook." What does it show?

2. How is a character's trait best judged?

3. "Why did he leave?" Where do you look?

4. "What happens next?" What do you use?

5. What is the theme of a story?

6. Smiling and humming shows which feeling?

7. "First... Then... Finally" helps with which question?

8. Can you assume facts not in the passage?

9. What is "setting"?

10. What shows mood best?

Answers: 1 nervousness, 2 actions and speech, 3 just before the action, 4 the last clues, 5 the lesson or big idea, 6 joy, 7 sequence, 8 no, 9 time and place, 10 adjectives and verbs.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Who, what, how did they feel?

Character shown by action and speech.

Emotion: body signals and mood words.

Motive: look just before the action.

Prediction: use the last clues.

Theme: what changes by the end.

Never imagine facts.
